results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.key_finding: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults aged 18-50 without immunocompromise: vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h or cefotaxime 2 g IV q4-6h). Neisseria meningitidis is exquisitely susceptible to penicillin and cephalosporins; targeted therapy is penicillin G or ceftriaxone once the organism is identified and susceptibility confirmed. Duration of therapy for meningococcal meningitis: 7 days.
results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis

results.authors: De Gans J, van de Beek D.
results.key_finding: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h for 4 days, started before or with the first dose of antibiotics, significantly reduced unfavorable outcomes and mortality in adults with bacterial meningitis, with greatest benefit seen in pneumococcal disease. Benefit in meningococcal meningitis was not statistically significant in this trial but adjunctive dexamethasone is recommended across all causes in high-income settings.
results.title: Dexamethasone in Adults with Bacterial Meningitis

results.authors: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, Dzupova O, et al.
results.key_finding: Adjunctive dexamethasone is recommended in all adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis in high-income countries. Meningococcal serogroup B, C, and W strains are responsible for the majority of epidemic disease; close contacts (household, dormitory) should receive chemoprophylaxis. Empiric vancomycin plus third-generation cephalosporin is appropriate until organism susceptibility is confirmed.
results.title: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults — ESCMID guidelines

output.summary: Empiric antibiotic regimens for adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis combine a third-generation cephalosporin with vancomycin pending susceptibility data. Neisseria meningitidis is typically highly susceptible to penicillin and cephalosporins, allowing early de-escalation to ceftriaxone monotherapy once confirmed. Adjunctive dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose is recommended in adults across all bacterial etiologies in high-income settings. Duration of therapy for confirmed meningococcal meningitis is 7 days. Close contacts in dormitory settings should receive chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone single dose) per public health guidance.

alternatives: If confirmed meningococcal meningitis with penicillin-susceptible strain (MIC ≤0.06 mcg/mL): de-escalate to penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h or ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h monotherapy for a 7-day total course.
If true IgE-mediated penicillin allergy were present: meropenem 2 g IV q8h is an acceptable alternative for meningococcal disease.
output.formulary_status: All three agents on formulary; no prior authorisation required for the acute indication.
interactions: Dexamethasone + Vancomycin: Corticosteroids reduce meningeal inflammation and may decrease CNS penetration of vancomycin by reducing blood-brain barrier permeability. Monitor for clinical and CSF sterilization if culture confirms a pathogen with elevated vancomycin MIC. Not a contraindication for empiric co-administration.

Dexamethasone + Ceftriaxone: No pharmacokinetic interaction. Dexamethasone does not meaningfully reduce CNS penetration of ceftriaxone; third-generation cephalosporins achieve excellent CSF concentrations independent of inflammation level.

warnings: Vancomycin: monitor renal function and serum trough levels or AUC-based dosing; nephrotoxicity risk is low in a patient with normal baseline creatinine.
Dexamethasone: may mask fever and signs of clinical deterioration; maintain close clinical monitoring during the 4-day course.
Dexamethasone: may cause transient hyperglycemia — monitor fingerstick glucose during the course.
Ceftriaxone: monitor for hypersensitivity. No penicillin allergy in this patient; cross-reactivity rate is low (<2%) even with documented penicillin allergy.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric IV antibiotics while awaiting LP, imaging, or any other test when meningococcal meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT dismiss petechial/purpuric rash as an allergic reaction or viral exanthem when accompanied by fever and meningismus — this triad requires urgent exclusion of meningococcal disease.
Do NOT perform CT before LP in this young, immunocompetent, neurologically intact patient; it would cause unsafe antibiotic delay without clinical justification.
Do NOT list analyze_csf as a harmful tool in the absence of mass effect; LP is the confirmatory test and is safe in this patient.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics; CNS penetration is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg loading dose + ceftriaxone 2 g IV) within 30-60 minutes of presentation; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP beyond the minimum time needed to collect blood cultures.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV (10 mg in standard adult dosing) before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose.

LP can proceed without prior CT in this young, immunocompetent, neurologically intact patient (no focal signs, no papilledema, GCS 15, no seizure) — proceed directly to lumbar puncture after blood cultures.
Place patient on droplet precautions immediately upon suspicion of meningococcal disease.

Notify public health authorities and initiate chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (dormitory roommates and close social contacts) with ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose, rifampin, or ceftriaxone IM.
Reassess antibiotic regimen when culture and PCR results confirm Neisseria meningitidis: de-escalate to ceftriaxone monotherapy if susceptible (7-day total course).
Monitor closely for signs of meningococcemia progression (purpura fulminans, hemodynamic instability, DIC) given petechial/purpuric rash and coagulopathy profile.

differential.key_features: Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash + fever + sepsis physiology in a young adult is the hallmark of meningococcal disease; meningismus here indicates CNS involvement, but the two can occur together or separately

Lymphocyte-predominant CSF, normal-to-mildly elevated glucose, less toxic appearance — this case has neutrophilic pleocytosis, very low glucose, and Gram-negative diplococci, which are inconsistent with viral disease
Pneumococcal meningitis is most common in adults; distinguished here by Gram-negative (not Gram-positive) diplococci on stain and PCR positivity for N. meningitidis

The petechial rash was initially misinterpreted as an allergic reaction; blanching maculopapular rash would support allergy, but non-blanching petechiae/purpura with meningismus and high fever indicate meningococcal disease until proven otherwise
Thunderclap headache and meningismus can mimic SAH; xanthochromic CSF and CT hemorrhage expected but absent; turbid CSF with neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose excludes this

key_clinical_evidence: The combination of fever, meningismus, and non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash in a young dormitory-residing adult constitutes a meningococcal emergency until proven otherwise — this triad demands immediate empiric antibiotics and droplet isolation.

The early rash was misinterpreted as an allergic reaction (intended red herring); non-blanching petechiae with fever and neck stiffness are pathognomonic of meningococcemia and must not be attributed to allergy or viral exanthem without thorough evaluation.

CT before LP is NOT required in this case: the patient is young, immunocompetent, alert (GCS 15), has no papilledema, no focal neurological deficits, and no seizure — all of the IDSA 2004 imaging-first criteria are absent. Ordering CT would introduce dangerous delay.

Gram-negative diplococci on CSF Gram stain combined with PCR positivity for Neisseria meningitidis provides high-confidence pathogen identification; empiric vancomycin can be de-escalated to ceftriaxone monotherapy once susceptibility is confirmed.

Dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces inflammation-driven morbidity; although its mortality benefit is greatest in pneumococcal disease, it is recommended empirically across all causes of bacterial meningitis.
Public health response is mandatory: close contacts in dormitory settings require chemoprophylaxis to prevent secondary cases; meningococcal disease is a notifiable condition.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Emma Hartley is a 19-year-old right-handed White woman and college freshman who presents to the emergency department via ambulance at 02:30 with an 8-hour history of rapidly worsening symptoms. She was in her usual state of health until yesterday evening when she developed an abrupt-onset, severe bifrontal and occipital headache she describes as the worst of her life, accompanied by high fever, chills, and malaise. She took 500 mg of acetaminophen around 19:00 with minimal relief. Approximately two hours later, her roommate noticed she was becoming increasingly irritable and photophobic, keeping the lights off and refusing to open her eyes. Around 22:00, her roommate observed a faint, diffuse reddish rash on her legs and abdomen. Initially attributed to a possible allergic reaction to laundry detergent or a new soap, the rash was not immediately alarming. By 01:00, the rash had spread and the lesions had become darker and more numerous, some appearing as flat, non-blanching purplish spots. The roommate called emergency services. On arrival by EMS, the patient was febrile to 39.6 degrees Celsius, tachycardic at 126 bpm, and hypotensive at 98/60. She complained of severe headache and neck pain and was noted to have marked nuchal rigidity. She was alert and conversational but extremely distressed. EMS initiated intravenous access and normal saline at 500 mL over 20 minutes during transport. On ED arrival she reports no prior episodes of similar symptoms, no recent sick contacts with confirmed meningitis, no history of recent antibiotic use, and no known immunodeficiency. She lives in a freshman dormitory with close shared bathroom and dining facilities. Her last meningococcal ACWY vaccination was at age 11 and no booster has been documented.
